source_refs.note: 11- Centrioles: a main subheading of 3.4 Structure of the cell, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 75-76.

blocks.text: In the cells of animals and most protists, centrioles are organelles associated with the assembly and organization of the fibres of cytoskeleton i.e., microtubules (including spindle fibres).

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: Centrioles are hollow and cylindrical organelles. A centriole is made of nine triplets of microtubules.

In eukaryotic cells centrioles occur in pairs. The two centrioles are located at right angles to one another near the nuclear envelope. In ciliated or flagellated cells centrioles are involved in the formation of cilia and flagella. Each cilium and flagellum is anchored by a centriole, known as basal body.

blocks.alt: Two centrioles lying at right angles to each other: one seen end-on as a ring of nine microtubule triplets, the other standing upright as a hollow cylinder.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.26: Two centrioles (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.26).

blocks.text: The cells of plants and fungi lack centrioles and basal bodies, and their microtubules and spindle fibres are organized from the structures of cytoplasm.
